sections.h2: Where does a Crawford County deed get recorded?
sections.html:
At the Crawford County Recorder's office in Bucyrus, the county seat. The recorder's website calls the office the official land records office for all real estate in Crawford County, and it lists 419-562-6961 as the number to call. The office follows sections 317.11 and 317.112 of the Ohio Revised Code, which set what a document must look like before staff accept it.

One local rule surprises people. According to the recorder's FAQ, a document that transfers real estate has to be approved first, and that process starts at the Crawford County Engineer's office, not at the recorder. The recorder also points out that its staff cannot give legal advice, so it suggests an attorney or title agency prepare the deed. Fill-in-the-blank forms exist, but the office stresses that the person submitting them is responsible for meeting every legal requirement.

sections.h2: How much does the Crawford County Recorder charge?
sections.html:
The recorder's fee page announces a $5 increase that took effect January 1, 2025 under Senate Bill 94, bringing the standard recording fee to $39 for the first two pages and $8 for each page after that. The office notes that each printed side counts as one page, and that $4 reference fees still apply when a document refers back to an earlier recording. The page-by-page figures it prints are:

Pages in the deedRecorder's fee
1 or 2$39.00
3$47.00
4$55.00
5$63.00
6$71.00
10$103.00

A few other items on the same schedule can come up in a sale. A release of a lien costs $4, a federal tax lien filing costs $5, and a document carrying a marginal notation adds $4 per notation to the regular fee. Plats and condominium drawings are priced by area, at $0.10 per square inch with a $40 minimum per page. The auditor and the treasurer collect their own amounts, which is why the recorder's checklist asks for separate checks.

sections.h2: What does the Crawford County Recorder want to see on a deed?
sections.html:
The recorder publishes an eleven-point guide, and these are the points that trip up sellers most often:

  • The document must be an original, signed and notarized
  • A deed prepared in Ohio must carry a prepared-by statement
  • It must include the complete legal description, which the office uses for geographic indexing
  • Later documents should cite the book and page of earlier recordings
  • Exhibits and schedules must be clearly identified
  • The preparer's name and address, a return address and a phone number for minor fixes should appear
  • A self-addressed stamped envelope gets the original back without postage charges

The office adds that it is the filer's job to make sure pages are legible enough to scan. Anything that fails the document standards is turned away, and a rejected deed means a second trip to Bucyrus.

When it indexes a deed, the office searches by legal description rather than street address. If you only have the house number, the recorder's FAQ says to find the owner name and transfer date through the Crawford County Auditor's search page first.

sections.h2: What does the Crawford County Auditor add to a sale?
sections.html:
The auditor sets the value that tax bills rest on and receives the conveyance paperwork. Its real estate page says property is revalued every three years under Ohio Department of Taxation rules, that taxes are figured on 35% of market value, and that Crawford County has 54 taxing districts, each with its own rate. No owner pays more than 10 mills of unvoted levies, and the voted portion depends on local elections.

Under section 319.202 the buyer files a value statement and the seller pays the conveyance fee, plus any county transfer tax that the commissioners have levied under section 322.02. The state fee is $1 or 10 cents per $100, whichever is greater, according to section 319.54. Ask the Crawford County Auditor which county rate applies, since the statute only caps it at 30 cents per $100.

The auditor's page also describes several items that matter to a seller:

  • Owners may contest a value from January 1 to March 31 before the Board of Revision
  • New construction or an improvement over $2,000 must be reported, and failure can bring a 50% penalty on the owner's taxes
  • Building permits are issued by the cities of Bucyrus and Galion, Jackson, Jefferson and Polk townships, and the villages of Crestline, New Washington, North Robinson and Chatfield
  • Farmland in the current agricultural use value program pays a one-time $25 enrollment fee
  • Manufactured home buyers have 30 days to register with the auditor, or face a $100 penalty

sections.h2: What is Crawford County like for a home seller?
sections.html:
Crawford County sits in north central Ohio. Wikipedia lists it as the fourth smallest county in the state by total area, at 403 square miles, with the Sandusky and Olentangy rivers draining it. Bucyrus is the county seat and largest city, and Galion is the other city. The county is named for Colonel William Crawford, and it makes up the Bucyrus micropolitan area. Neighbors are Seneca, Huron, Richland, Morrow, Marion and Wyandot counties.

The county's population peaked at 50,364 in 1970 and counted 42,025 in 2020, with the Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate at 41,896. Crestline, which has its own public library alongside those in Bucyrus and Galion, is one of the villages that file deeds in the same Bucyrus office. In the 2020 census, 65.9% of residents lived in urban areas and 34.1% in rural areas, a split that explains why a Bucyrus lot and a township farmhouse can be priced so differently.

sections.h2: How do Crawford County homes compare on the numbers?
sections.html:
The Census Bureau's QuickFacts table gives the following for Crawford County:

  • Median value of an owner-occupied home: $136,700 for 2020 to 2024
  • Owner-occupied rate: 73.1%
  • Housing units: 19,813, with 18,059 households
  • Median gross rent: $794
  • Median household income: $58,044, with 11.2% of people in poverty
  • Building permits in 2025: 3
  • Median owner cost with a mortgage: $1,081 a month, and $487 without one

A count of just three permits for 2025 suggests how little new building the county sees. Most sales are existing houses, many of them older. A written cash offer or a local appraisal can price one of those homes more reliably than a countywide median can.

sections.h2: What should be settled before heading to Bucyrus?
sections.html:
The recorder's FAQ makes clear that it does not release liens. It records them, and the Treasurer or the Clerk of Courts handles the underlying tax and court filings. That means a seller should sort out the following with the right office before the deed is filed:

  • Ask the County Treasurer for the unpaid tax figure so the title company can pay it from the proceeds
  • Ask a lender to file a release of any old mortgage, since the recorder only records it
  • Check with the Clerk of Courts for judgments tied to the owner
  • Ask the County Engineer's office about the transfer approval step
  • Match the legal description to the one on your last deed

The same steps apply when the buyer is paying cash and the house is sold as-is.

faqs.q: What is the phone number for the Crawford County Recorder?
faqs.a: The office number printed on the recorder's website is 419-562-6961. The office is in Bucyrus.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to record a three-page deed in Crawford County?
faqs.a: The recorder's fee table prints $47.00 for three pages. That is $39 for the first two pages and $8 for the third, before any other charges the document triggers.

faqs.q: Does the recorder remove liens from my title?
faqs.a: No. The office only records certain liens and says it does not remove or release them. Property tax liens go through the County Treasurer, and court matters through the Clerk of Courts.

faqs.q: Where does the transfer process start in Crawford County?
faqs.a: At the County Engineer's office, according to the recorder's FAQ. A document that transfers real estate has to be approved there before it moves on.

faqs.q: Can I search records by street address at the recorder?
faqs.a: Not directly. The recorder indexes by legal description, so look up the owner name or transfer date on the County Auditor's search page if you only have an address.
